title: Finding the Lowest Common Ancestor in a BST

phrases.explanation: The deepest node in a tree that is an ancestor of both given nodes
To trace through a specific test case step by step to verify understanding
To take advantage of the fact that left children are smaller and right children are larger than the current node
To reduce the range of possible answers by eliminating impossible candidates
The simplest scenario in a recursive solution where the answer is returned directly without further recursion

technical_terms.definition: A binary tree where every node's left subtree contains only smaller values and the right subtree contains only larger values
The deepest node in the tree that has both target nodes as descendants, where a node can be a descendant of itself
A technique that solves a problem by calling the same function on smaller subtrees until a base case is reached
A technique that uses a loop instead of recursion to walk through the tree one node at a time
The sequence of nodes from the root down to a given target node in the tree

concept: Given a binary search tree and two nodes that exist in the tree, find their lowest common ancestor. The lowest common ancestor is the deepest node that has both given nodes as descendants, where a node is allowed to be a descendant of itself.

solutions.label: Path Comparison
solutions.summary: Find the path from the root to each target node, then compare the two paths to find the last common node.

solutions.label: Recursive BST Traversal
solutions.summary: Recursively use BST ordering to decide whether to go left, right, or return the current node as the answer.

solutions.label: Iterative BST Traversal
solutions.summary: Iteratively traverse the BST using the same logic as the recursive approach, eliminating the call stack overhead.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: You're given a binary search tree and two nodes, p and q, that are guaranteed to exist in the tree. Find their lowest common ancestor. A node can be a descendant of itself.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: So I need to find the deepest node that is an ancestor of both p and q. Can the two nodes be the same node?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Good question. The two nodes will always be distinct, and both are guaranteed to exist in the tree. The tree has unique values and at least two nodes.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Got it. And should I return the node itself or just its value?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Return the tree node object. For example, in a BST with root six, if p is two and q is eight, the answer is node six since it's the deepest node that is an ancestor of both.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Understood. So I have a BST with unique values, two distinct nodes that exist in it, and I return their lowest common ancestor node. Let me think about approaches.

sections.title: Path Comparison
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    style N6 fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style N2 fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style N4 fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style N5 fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    N6[6] --> N2[2]
    N6 --> N8[8]
    N2 --> N0[0]
    N2 --> N4[4]
    N4 --> N3[3]
    N4 --> N5[5]
    N8 --> N7[7]
    N8 --> N9[9]
    P1["Path to 2: 6 → 2"] -.-> N6
    P2["Path to 5: 6 → 2 → 4 → 5"] -.-> N6
    ANS["Last common: 2"] -.-> N2

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: My first idea is a path comparison approach. I'll find the path from the root to p and the path from the root to q, storing each in a list. Then I compare the two lists and find the last node they share.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Let's walk through an example. If p is two and q is five in our BST rooted at six, what happens?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The path to two is six then two. The path to five is six, two, four, five. Comparing these, both share six and two. The last common node is two, so that's our answer.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: What's the complexity?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Time is O of n in the worst case for a skewed tree since finding each path could visit every node. Space is also O of n to store the two paths. This works, but we're not using the BST property efficiently.

sections.title: Recursive BST Traversal
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    style N6 fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style N2 fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    N6["6: p=2 < 6, q=5 < 6 → go left"] --> N2["2: p=2 ≤ 2 ≤ q=5 → split point!"]
    N6 --> N8[8]
    N2 --> N0[0]
    N2 --> N4[4]
    N4 --> N3[3]
    N4 --> N5[5]
    N8 --> N7[7]
    N8 --> N9[9]
    RES["Return node 2"] -.-> N2

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: I can leverage the BST property. If both p and q are smaller than the current node, the ancestor must be in the left subtree. If both are larger, it's in the right subtree. Otherwise, the current node is the split point and that's our answer.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Walk through the same example with p equals two and q equals five.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: At node six, both two and five are less than six, so I recurse left. At node two, two is equal to two and five is greater than two. They don't both go the same direction, so node two is the split point. Return two.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Great. What about complexity?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Time is O of h where h is the height of the tree, since we only visit one node per level. Space is also O of h due to the recursion call stack. For a balanced tree, h is log n, which is much better.

sections.title: Iterative BST Traversal
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    style N6 fill:#fb923c,color:#fff
    style N2 fill:#fb923c,color:#fff
    N6["6: both < 6 → move left"] --> N2["2: split → answer!"]
    N6 --> N8[8]
    N2 --> N0[0]
    N2 --> N4[4]
    N4 --> N3[3]
    N4 --> N5[5]
    N8 --> N7[7]
    N8 --> N9[9]
    RES["Return node 2, O of 1 space"] -.-> N2

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The recursive approach has O of h space from the call stack. I can convert it to an iterative solution using a while loop. I start at the root and keep moving left or right based on the same BST comparison logic.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: How does the loop work step by step?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: I set current to root. While current is not null, if both p and q values are less than current, I move current to current dot left. If both are greater, I move to current dot right. Otherwise, I return current because that's the split point.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: With p equals two and q equals five, at node six both are smaller so I move left. At node two, they split, so I return two. Time is O of h, and now space is O of one since there's no recursion.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Nice progression. You went from path comparison at O of n time and space, to recursive BST traversal at O of h time and space, then to iterative with O of h time and O of one space.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The key insight is that in a BST, the lowest common ancestor is the node where p and q split into different subtrees. Once you see that, the solution becomes a simple traversal from root to the split point.
